doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Jazz funeral tradition and its erosion, Percy Humphrey's funeral
summary: He explains burial band customs, laments kid bands and crowds diluting the tradition, citing Percy Humphrey's funeral.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Something else, the brass bands were important as a vehicle for the development of this music. Talk to us about particularly the African-American tradition of the burial bands.

Well it’s a belief in New Orleans that I mean when you die, it’s not like the end then. So it’s kind of like a party that we give the guy a sendoff into his next thing, whatever that is. I mean whatever —

Yeah, his next gig. I like the way you said that, next gig. So like on the way we give respect and all of those kinds of things to the body on the way to the cemetery. We play dirges and quite naturally the family is sad, people who knew this person is sad, and when we get to the cemetery, we play a nice slow hymn, some kind of hymn, “What a Friend We Have in Jesus,” or “Goodbye Charlie” or whatever it’s going to be. And then we immediately turn around and start the celebration. Because this guy has gone on somewhere else now. And I think that’s a really great way of looking at it, rather than dwelling upon, oh man, my brother’s dead or whoever it is. The family doesn’t take part usually in the celebration, quite naturally. But the rest of the people just kind of turn him loose and set him free to do whatever’s next.
And the music is a large part of that. It helps them do that.

Oh, yeah. So we hit up one of those real lively songs with a bass drum. We’re kind of losing that in New Orleans. Because that was a very, very respectful tradition at one time. But then all of a sudden it got to be less and less organized. Then you started getting a lot of people who wanted to participate, which is nice, it’s nice people want to participate in

it, but as they participate, the real tradition is being destroyed, or like diluted. And then, all of a sudden like these kid bands started coming out, in tee shirts and jeans. Like whenever we had a funeral parade, everyone was dressed in a black or dark suit, white shirt and tie. Black hat, you know. That’s the way that tradition went. But now, everybody’s got the baseball cap backwards, and you know and I mean the tradition is in serious threat there. Now and then we have a real, traditional New Orleans funeral. But it’s because these people are responding more to these young kid’s bands, which is high energy, but they don’t have the proper respect for the tradition or for the purpose of the funeral parade itself. You know, and not to mention, they don’t really know those hymns. Because they don’t respect that kind of music. And I mean it’s just like, you know, this is a fast world now. Everything is going really, really fast. So —
In other words, continuity and change have to be balanced.

Yes. They have to be. That’s a great way of putting that. They have to be balanced. And if they’re not balanced, we’re going to destroy that tradition, which is in a big threat now. We just buried an old guy from the Preservation Hall, Mr. Percy Humphrey. And you know we tried to keep it as a traditional jazz funeral. But it was, a lot of people started coming in there, some lady playing the flute with tights and you know, a leotard and all this kind of crazy stuff you know. I mean she’s got a right to express herself. But that’s not part of that thing. And we didn’t walk too far. The weather was really bad. And everyone, the crowd was like getting into the band, getting between the band and you can’t play that way, man. Because is doesn’t take but one elbow, you know, on the end of your horn, to knock your teeth out, and that’s the end. Because it’s just the end that’s it. So you have to be very careful with stuff like that. And if they don’t respect the band, you know, or the tradition, it’s going to be destroyed. And a lot of guys were like hardly playing because so many people were walking in and out of the band.
